## Course Overview

[View the Course Introduction slides](course-intro/index.html){target="_blank"}

This course teaches you how to think about **cause and effect** in complex health systems. Across 10 chapters, you will build a complete toolkit for causal reasoning — from drawing simple diagrams to making real decisions about where to invest resources to save the most lives.

The ideas come from *Inference and Intervention: Causal Models for Business Analysis* (Ryall & Bramson, 2014), but every example is new and grounded in real maternal and newborn health (MNH) challenges in **Ethiopia, Rwanda, Kenya, and Tanzania** — using publicly available data.

::: {.callout-box}
**The central message:** Causal models are **practical tools** for answering the questions that matter most in global health: *Where should we invest? What should we do? How do we know it will work?*
:::

## What You Will Learn

By the end of this course, you will be able to:

1. **Draw a causal diagram** (DAG) from interviews and program knowledge (Chapters 1--3)
2. **Put numbers on the arrows** using data and expert judgment (Chapters 4--5)
3. **Spot common reasoning traps** like Simpson's Paradox (Chapter 6)
4. **Make better decisions** about where to invest resources (Chapters 7--8)
5. **Think strategically** about how other people will respond (Chapter 9)
6. **Use data to check your model** — and improve it (Chapter 10)

## Chapters

### Part 1: Draw the Picture

| Chapter | Title | What You Will Learn |
|---------|-------|---------------------|
| 1 | [Introduction to Causal Analysis](chapters/ch01.qmd) | Why correlation is not causation; three traps to avoid |

| 3 | [The MNH Diagnostic Case Study](chapters/ch03.qmd) | Building a diagram step by step through interviews |

| Chapter | Title | What You Will Learn |
|---------|-------|---------------------|
| 4 | [Quantitative Causal Models](chapters/ch04.qmd) | Putting numbers on your diagram; Bayes' rule made simple |
| 5 | [Situational Analysis](chapters/ch05.qmd) | Updating your beliefs when you learn new information |
| 6 | [Simpson's Paradox & Cost-Effectiveness](chapters/ch06.qmd) | When combined data lies — and how to spot it |

### Part 3: Make Decisions

| Chapter | Title | What You Will Learn |
|---------|-------|---------------------|
| 7 | [Decision Analysis & Value of Information](chapters/ch07.qmd) | Choosing between options; the difference between watching and doing |
| 8 | [Multi-Country Resource Allocation](chapters/ch08.qmd) | Splitting a budget across countries under uncertainty |
| 9 | [Game Theory & Strategic Interactions](chapters/ch09.qmd) | What happens when other people react to your decisions |

## The Four Countries

All examples draw from publicly available data about MNH challenges in:

| Country | Key Context |
|---------|-------------|
| **Ethiopia** | ~40,000 Health Extension Workers; MMR ~267/100K (WHO); major regional variation |
| **Rwanda** | ~58,000 community health workers; Mutuelle de Santé (universal health insurance); 94%+ facility delivery |
| **Kenya** | 47 devolved counties; ~89% facility delivery but high county-level variation; MMR ~342/100K |
| **Tanzania** | 26 regions; DHIS2/GOTHOMIS data system at most facilities; ~55% health workforce shortage |

## Prerequisites

- **Curiosity about how the world works.** No math background needed.
- Some basic familiarity with R programming is helpful but not required (see the [R Setup](r-setup.qmd) page)
- No prior knowledge of causal inference or statistics is assumed

## Textbook

Ryall, M. D., & Bramson, A. (2014). *Inference and Intervention: Causal Models for Business Analysis*. Routledge.

::: {.callout-box .green}
**Note:** We teach the same core concepts from the textbook but use entirely new examples drawn from public MNH data — not the business examples from the book.
:::
